title: How long can you leave a tampon in? A safety guide
description: How long can you leave a tampon in? Learn when to change your tampon, whether you can sleep with one in, and how to reduce your risk of toxic shock syndrome.
imageAlt: Mochi, a pink mascot, pointing at a small alarm clock next to a box of tampons
intro: You can leave a tampon in for 4 to 8 hours, but never longer than 8 hours, even if your flow is light. Changing your tampon regularly and choosing the lowest absorbency you need can help reduce your risk of toxic shock syndrome (TSS), a rare but serious condition. Here's how to manage tampon changes throughout your day and night.

how-long.title: How long can you leave a tampon in?

paragraphs.first: You should change your tampon every 4 to 8 hours, regardless of how much you are bleeding. The FDA advises never wearing a single tampon for more than 8 hours. This applies to every tampon, whether it is light, regular, super or super plus, and even if it is not completely saturated.
paragraphs.second: According to Cleveland Clinic, many healthcare professionals recommend changing your tampon every 4 to 6 hours, or more frequently on heavier days. Eight hours is the maximum, not a target. You can always change your tampon earlier if you are leaking, feeling uncomfortable or simply prefer to use a fresh one.
paragraphs.third: The clock starts again every time you insert a new tampon. If you tend to forget when you last changed yours, setting a reminder on your phone can help. You can also use Mochi's change reminder to keep track of when your next change is due without having to remember the time yourself.

overnight.title: Can you sleep with a tampon in?

paragraphs.first: You can sleep with a tampon in under the FDA's wearing-time guidance, provided you remove it within 8 hours of insertion. However, Health Canada advises against using tampons overnight altogether. Using a pad or period underwear while you sleep is a simple way to avoid accidentally exceeding the recommended wearing time.
paragraphs.second: If you choose to wear a tampon overnight, insert a fresh one just before going to bed and remove it as soon as you wake up, within the 8-hour limit. Remember that the time you spend getting ready for bed or lying awake also counts towards those 8 hours.
paragraphs.third: If you usually sleep for more than 8 hours, enjoy sleeping in on weekends or are unsure when you will wake up, choose an overnight pad or period underwear instead. There is no need to interrupt your sleep to change a tampon when you have another comfortable option available.

heavy-and-light-flow.title: How long can you leave a tampon in on heavy and light days?

paragraphs.first: On heavy flow days, you may need to change your tampon every 4 hours or sooner. On light flow days, you can wear one for up to 8 hours, but never beyond that limit. The FDA recommends using the lowest absorbency that comfortably manages your menstrual flow, rather than choosing a higher absorbency to make a tampon last longer.
paragraphs.second: When your flow is heavy, pay attention to signs that your tampon may be becoming saturated. Leaking or blood appearing on the tampon string can be clues that it is time for a change, although a stained string alone does not necessarily mean the tampon is full. You do not need to wait until your next scheduled change.
paragraphs.third: When your flow is light, a tampon may still feel relatively dry when you remove it. If removal regularly feels dry or uncomfortable, you may be using a higher absorbency than you need. Try switching to a lighter tampon, a pad or period underwear instead of leaving the tampon in longer. Always follow the 8-hour maximum.

swimming-and-peeing.title: Can you swim, shower and pee with a tampon in?

paragraphs.first: Yes, you can swim, shower and pee while wearing a tampon. You do not need to remove it every time you get into the water or use the bathroom. The same safety rule applies to all these activities: change your tampon every 4 to 8 hours and never leave it in for longer than 8 hours.
paragraphs.second: After swimming, you may want to change your tampon if it feels damp or uncomfortable. You can also put in a fresh tampon before getting into the pool or sea if your next change is nearly due. Remember that swimming and showering do not restart the 8-hour clock. Only inserting a new tampon does.
paragraphs.third: You can pee with a tampon in because the tampon sits inside your vagina, while urine leaves your body through a separate opening called the urethra. If you want to keep the string dry, gently hold it to one side while you pee. You can change your tampon if the string gets wet. Always wash your hands before and after changing your tampon.

toxic-shock-syndrome.title: What is toxic shock syndrome and how long does it take?

paragraphs.first: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a rare but potentially life-threatening condition caused by toxins produced by certain bacteria. There is no exact number of hours you can wear a tampon before developing toxic shock syndrome. The risk increases when tampons are left in too long, but TSS can also develop within the recommended wearing time.
paragraphs.second: According to the NHS, symptoms of toxic shock syndrome can develop quickly. They may initially feel similar to the flu or a stomach illness. Knowing what to look for can help you seek medical care early. The FDA and NHS identify the following symptoms as possible warning signs of TSS.
paragraphs.third: If you are wearing a tampon and develop any of these symptoms, remove it and seek urgent medical advice. Tell the healthcare professional that you have been using tampons. Do not wait for all the symptoms to appear or for them to become more severe. TSS is rare, but suspected cases need prompt medical attention.

items.fever: A sudden high fever, chills or feeling shivery.
items.rash: A skin rash that may feel rough like sandpaper.

toxic-shock-syndrome.note: According to the NHS, call emergency services immediately if you experience confusion, difficulty breathing, a rash that does not fade when pressed, or blue, grey or blotchy skin or lips.

left-in-too-long.title: What if you accidentally left a tampon in for 12 hours, 24 hours or longer?

paragraphs.first: If you accidentally left a tampon in for 12 hours, 24 hours or longer, remove it as soon as you remember. Try not to panic. Toxic shock syndrome is rare, and exceeding the recommended wearing time does not automatically mean you will develop it. However, leaving a tampon in too long increases your risk.
paragraphs.second: After removing the tampon, pay attention to how you feel over the next few days. Watch for symptoms of toxic shock syndrome, including a sudden fever, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle aches, a rash or dizziness. If any of these symptoms develop, seek urgent medical advice and explain how long the tampon was left in.
paragraphs.third: If you cannot find the tampon or are unable to remove it yourself, contact a doctor or nurse promptly. You should also seek medical advice if you notice unusual vaginal discharge, an unpleasant smell or pelvic pain. If you develop a fever or other possible symptoms of toxic shock syndrome, seek urgent medical help.
paragraphs.fourth: A forgotten or difficult-to-remove tampon is a common situation that healthcare professionals are familiar with. A doctor or nurse can usually locate and remove it quickly. You do not need to feel embarrassed about asking for help. For future tampon changes, a phone alarm or Mochi's change reminder can help you stay within the recommended 8-hour limit.

tampon-or-pad.title: When is a pad or period underwear the better choice?

paragraphs.first: A pad or period underwear is a better choice when you expect to sleep for more than 8 hours, when your flow is very light or when removing a tampon feels dry or uncomfortable. Health Canada also recommends avoiding tampons altogether if you have ever had toxic shock syndrome (TSS).
paragraphs.second: You do not have to choose between tampons and pads for your entire period. Health Canada recommends alternating between tampons and pads. You might prefer a tampon during the day, a pad at night and period underwear towards the end of your period. Choose whatever feels comfortable and suits your routine.

items.long-nights: Choose a pad or period underwear if you expect to sleep for longer than 8 hours.
items.light-flow: Switch to a pad or period underwear when your flow is too light for comfortable tampon removal.
items.previous-tss: Avoid tampons if you have previously had toxic shock syndrome.
items.alternating: Alternate between tampons and pads throughout your period.

change-reminder.title: How can you remember to change your tampon?

paragraphs.first: The easiest way to remember to change your tampon is to set a reminder as soon as you insert it. Aim to change it every 4 to 8 hours, or sooner on heavier days. Each time you put in a fresh tampon, restart your reminder so it reflects the new insertion time.
paragraphs.second: Mochi is a free, private period tracker for iPhone with a built-in change reminder. It gently nudges you when it is time for a change and displays a discreet countdown so you can check how much time is left. It works offline, requires no account and keeps your cycle data on your iPhone unless you enable optional backup.
paragraphs.third: A reminder is a helpful way to manage tampon changes, but you should never wait for an alert if you feel unwell. If you develop a sudden fever, vomiting, diarrhea, a rash or dizziness while wearing a tampon, remove it and seek urgent medical advice. Possible symptoms of toxic shock syndrome need prompt attention, regardless of how long you have been wearing your tampon.

eight-hours.question: Is it safe to leave a tampon in for 8 hours?
eight-hours.answer: Eight hours is within the FDA's recommended wearing time, but it is the maximum, not the ideal target. Change your tampon every 4 to 8 hours, or sooner if it becomes full or uncomfortable.

six-hours.question: Is 6 hours too long to wear a tampon?
six-hours.answer: No, wearing a tampon for 6 hours is within the recommended safety guidelines. According to Cleveland Clinic, many healthcare professionals suggest changing tampons every 4 to 6 hours, with more frequent changes on heavier days.

is-it-full.question: How can I tell if a tampon is full?
is-it-full.answer: Leaking or blood on the tampon string may indicate that your tampon is becoming full, although a stained string alone is not a reliable sign. Change it if you notice leaking, and never wait longer than 8 hours, even if it does not seem full.

tss-speed.question: How quickly does TSS develop?
tss-speed.answer: There is no fixed number of hours after inserting a tampon at which toxic shock syndrome develops. The NHS explains that symptoms can appear quickly, and the risk associated with tampon use increases when a tampon is left in too long. If you develop possible symptoms, remove your tampon and seek urgent medical advice.

tss-obvious.question: Would it be obvious if I had TSS?
tss-obvious.answer: Not necessarily, because early symptoms of toxic shock syndrome can resemble the flu or a stomach illness. A sudden fever, muscle aches, vomiting, diarrhea, a rash or dizziness can be warning signs. Remove your tampon and seek urgent medical advice if you develop these symptoms, rather than waiting for them to become more obvious.

stuck-tampon.question: How would you know if a tampon is stuck or forgotten?
stuck-tampon.answer: An unusual vaginal smell, unexpected discharge or pelvic discomfort may be signs of a forgotten tampon, although you may not notice any symptoms. If you think a tampon is still inside your vagina and cannot find or remove it, contact a doctor or nurse promptly. Seek urgent medical help if you also develop a fever or other possible symptoms of TSS.

still-wet.question: Why am I still wet with a tampon in?
still-wet.answer: Feeling wet while wearing a tampon can be due to normal vaginal moisture, discharge or menstrual blood leaking past the tampon. A tampon absorbs menstrual flow but does not keep the entire vaginal area dry. If you are leaking, consider changing your tampon while continuing to use the lowest absorbency that meets your needs.

pull-out.question: Is it better to pull a tampon out fast or slowly?
pull-out.answer: It is generally more comfortable to remove a tampon slowly and gently, using steady pressure on the string rather than pulling suddenly. If removal regularly feels dry or uncomfortable, consider using a lower absorbency or switching to a pad. If you cannot remove the tampon, contact a healthcare professional rather than forcing it.
